vignette:
Leilani, a 66-year-old shopowner, remembers the evening with a fragmented horror, like a dream she can’t quite shake but also can’t fully grasp. It had been nearly two years since the incident, a chaotic night when her small island goods shop became an accidental flashpoint during a street protest that escalated violently. She had been trying to secure her storefront when the riot police moved in, a wall of dark uniforms and flashing lights. She recalls the overwhelming sensation of being pinned against the wall of her own shop, the rough fabric of a uniform against her cheek, the shouts and the blinding glare of a handheld light directly in her face. The world had spun then, a dizzying, terrifying sensation that made her feel untethered from her own body. Certain details remain stubbornly out of reach, no matter how hard she tries to piece them together; there are simply parts of the event that she cannot remember, as if her mind has drawn a curtain. When she does try to recount it, the words often fail her, the experience so extreme that it is hard to believe it actually happened to her, almost like a story told by someone else.

Now, that dizzying sensation has become a persistent ghost. When she feels a sudden lightness in her head, even just from standing up too quickly in her shop, a wave of panic washes over her, bringing with it the cold dread of that night. The specific time of day the police had descended, just as dusk was deepening into night, has become another potent trigger. As the clock approaches 7 PM, a familiar anxiety tightens in her chest. She finds herself rushing to close her shop, pulling down the blinds and locking the door well before she used to, even though the evening hours were often her busiest. The thought of being in the dark, especially alone, fills her with an overwhelming fear, a direct echo of her vulnerability that night. She has even started to keep her shop’s interior lights blazing bright, even on cloudy days, a subconscious effort to push back the encroaching shadows.

The memory of being scrutinized by the officers, their faces obscured by helmets, has left her with an acute sensitivity to being watched. In her small shop, when a customer lingers a little too long at a display, or when she feels a pair of eyes on her as she rings up a purchase, Leilani’s heart begins to pound. She finds herself nervously adjusting her glasses, her gaze darting, convinced that she is being judged or, worse, targeted again.

Over the past months, these fears have woven themselves deeply into the fabric of her life. The annual town festival, which falls around the anniversary of the incident, now brings a wave of dread rather than excitement. She avoids the main street entirely on those days, even if it means missing out on potential business. To cope with the escalating anxiety and the profound sense of helplessness, Leilani has developed a habit of compulsive spending. She finds herself buying large quantities of new inventory for her shop that she doesn’t necessarily need, or ordering expensive, unnecessary items online, a fleeting distraction and comfort from the relentless internal turmoil. This has begun to strain her small business’s finances, adding another layer of worry.

Leilani often scrutinizes her own reactions, her racing heart, the sudden waves of panic, the difficulty in articulating her trauma. She has come to believe that her inability to move past the event is proof that she is inadequate, that she is simply a lousy coper. The most terrifying thought that has begun to plague her is the fear that her mind is failing her, that her reactions since the event mean that she is going crazy. It was this creeping dread, the feeling that she was losing control not just of her shop but of herself, that finally pushed Leilani to seek help, hoping someone could explain why her world still felt so broken.
